findings.finding: Insights: f(n)=min_{a+b+c=n} lcm(a,b,c). Use triple (1,2,n‑3): lcm= n‑3 if n odd, 2(n‑3) if n even; this is optimal for all n≥6. Hence f(n)=n‑3 for odd n, =2(n‑3) for even n. Then g(c)=⌊T·f(M+c)/M⌋/T with T=2025!, M=3^T. Since f(M+c)≈M (odd/even), T·f/M≈T·(≈1) giving floor =T‑1 or T‑2 etc. Compute each g(c) via parity of M+c (M odd, so parity = c odd). Sum six values → rational p/q; find p+q mod 99991. Pitfall: ensure f formula holds for huge n; verify no smaller lcm exists.

Insights: f(n)=min lcm(a,b,c) with a+b+c=n ⇒ f(n)=n·min_{s|n, s≥6} r(s) where r(s)=f(s)/s. Computed r(s) for s≤200: smallest is 6/11 (s multiple 11), next 4/7 (s multiple 7), then 3/5 (s multiple 10).  

M=3^{2025!} ⇒ M≡1 (mod p) for any prime p≤2025, p≠3. Thus M+c≡1+c (mod p).  

c‑values: 0, 4M (→5M), 1848374, 10162574, 265710644, 44636594.  
- M: divisors are powers of 3 ⇒ smallest s≥6 is 9, r=2/3 ⇒ f(M)=2/3·M.  
- 5M: still has 9 ⇒ r=2/3 ⇒ f(5M)=2/3·5M.  
- Other c’s: even and ≡4 (mod 5) ⇒ M+c divisible by 2·5=10, not by 7 or 11 ⇒ minimal r=3/5 ⇒ f(M+c)=3/5·(M+c).  

Since 2025! is divisible by 3,5, the floors give exact values:  
g(0)=2/3, g(4M)=10/3, each other g=3/5.  

Sum = 2/3+10/3+4·3/5 = 4+12/5 = 32/5 ⇒ p+q=32+5=37.  

Answer: 37.   (Pitfall: ensure s≥6; 5 alone can’t be used.)

Insights: f(n)=min lcm(a,b,c) with a+b+c=n. For any k, max sum of two proper divisors ≤k/2+k/3=5k/6 ⇒ f(n)/n≥6/11, equality when k multiple of 6 (a=k/2,b=k/3). Thus for huge M=3^{T}, any n≈M has f(n)<M ⇒ floor(f/M)=0. Only n=5M gives floor=3 (since f(5M)=10/3 M).  

Define g(c)=⌊T·f(M+c)/M⌋/T. Write f(M+c)=kM+r (0≤r<M). Then g(c)=k+⌊T·r/M⌋/T. For c=0,4M,1848374,10162574,265710644,44636594 we have k’s: 0,3,0,0,0,0.  

Compute r’s:  
- r₀=f(M)=2/3 M →⌊T·r₀/M⌋=⌊2T/3⌋=2T/3 (T divisible by 3).  
- r₁=f(5M)−3M=M/3 →⌊T·r₁/M⌋=⌊T/3⌋=T/3.  
- For the four small‑c terms, n≈M, the optimal triple is (k/2,k/3,k) with k≈6n/11≈6M/11, giving r≈(6/11)M. Hence ⌊T·r/M⌋≈⌊6T/11⌋=6T/11 (T divisible by 11).  

Thus S=2T/3+T/3+4·(6T/11)=2T+24T/11= (22T+24T)/11=46T/11.  

Total sum = (3T+S)/T = 3+46/11 = (33+46)/11 =79/11. Reduce → p=79,q=11.  

Answer: (79+11) mod 99991 = 90.

Insights: f(n)=min lcm(a,b,c) with a+b+c=n ⇒ f(n)=n·min_{s|n}R(s), R(s)=min lcm/s. Smallest R(s) values (odd s): 6/11 (s multiple 11), 4/7 (s 7), 10/17 (s 17), 16/25 (s 25), 2/3 (s 9), 4/5 (s 15)… For M=3^K, M≡1 (mod p≠3, p≤2025). Thus M+c’s odd divisors = odd divisors of c+1 (except c=0,4M). Compute c+1 factorizations: 1848375,10162575 have 25 ⇒ R=16/25; 265710645 has 9 ⇒ R=2/3; 44636595 has 15 ⇒ R=4/5; M,5M have 9 ⇒ R=2/3. g(c)=⌊2025!·R·(1+c/M)⌋/2025!; for c≪M term negligible, for 4M term adds factor 5. Hence g: 2/3, 10/3, 16/25, 16/25, 2/3, 4/5. Sum = 506/75 ⇒ p+q≡581 (mod 99991). Pitfalls: assume M≡1 mod small primes, ignore 3‑mod case, ensure s≥6, handle 4M term.

Insights: f(N)=min LCM(a,b,c) with a+b+c=N. For any N, f(N)≥⌈6N/11⌉ (from a,b≤N/2,N/3). Equality holds when N≡0 (mod 11) using (2k,3k,6k). For odd N (our six cases) N≡1,5,2,3,4,6 (mod 11); f(N)=⌈6N/11⌉+Δ(r) where Δ depends only on r (residue mod 11). Compute Δ(r) by checking small N (≤200) for each r. Then f(M+c)=⌈6(M+c)/11⌉+Δ(r). Since M≡1 (mod 11), r=(c+1) mod 11. Use 2025!≫M to get g(c)=⌊2025!·f(M+c)/M⌋/2025!≈f(M+c)/M. Sum g(c) = Σ(⌈6/11⌉+Δ(r)/M)≈6·6/11+ΣΔ(r)/M. Only Δ terms matter after scaling by 2025!. Compute p/q, then (p+q) mod 99991. Pitfalls: ensure Δ correct for each residue; handle large M via modular arithmetic; g(c) uses floor, but error <1/2025! negligible.

Insights: f(n)=min lcm(a,b,c) with a+b+c=n ⇒ f(n)=n·min_{S|n} (L_S/S) where L_S is min lcm for sum S. Global min L/S=6/11 (S multiple 11). M=3^{2025!}≡1 (mod p) for p≤2025, p≠3. Compute smallest S|N (N=M+c) giving lowest L/S. Results: N=M,5M ⇒ S=9, L/S=2/3. N=M+1848374 ⇒ S=25, L/S=16/25. N=M+10162574 ⇒ S=47, L/S=30/47. N=M+265710644 ⇒ S=97, L/S=64/97. N=M+44636594 ⇒ S=167, L/S=110/167. g(c)=floor(2025!·ratio·(1+c/M))/2025!; for tiny c, ratio unchanged; for c=4M factor 5 ⇒ g=5·2/3=10/3. Sum = 2/3+10/3+16/25+30/47+64/97+110/167 = 224414944/57101475. (p+q) mod 99991 = 41754. Pitfalls: treat 4M factor 5, ensure denominators divide 2025!.

Insights: f(n)=min_{a+b+c=n}LCM(a,b,c)=n·min_{s|n}(f(s)/s). Base ratios from primitive triples: 6/11 (s=11), 4/7 (7), 10/17 (17), 3/5 (10), 14/23 (23), … . For any N, f(N)=N·r where r is smallest ratio among those s dividing N. Since M=3^{2025!}≡1 (mod s) for s∤3, N=M+c ⇒ N≡1+c (mod s). For s a power of 3, N≡c (mod s). Test each base s (≤~200) for divisibility of each N (c=0,4M,1848374,…). Compute r, then g(c)=⌊2025!·N·r/M⌋/2025!. For N≈M, ⌊2025!·r⌋/2025!≈r (tiny δ ignored). Sum six g’s → rational p/q; output (p+q) mod 99991. Pitfall: ensure s|N test uses correct residue (1+c or c) and include s=3‑powers. Use exact fractions; reduce final p/q before mod.

Insights: f(n)=min lcm(a,b,c) with a+b+c=n ⇒ f(n)=n·min_{s|n, s≥6} f(s)/s. Minimal ratios: 6/11 (s multiple 11), 4/7 (s multiple 7), 3/5 (s=10), 16/25 (s=25), 64/97, 68/103,… 2025! contains all denominators.  

M=3^{2025!}, M≡1 (mod p) for any p≤2025, p≠3.  

c’s: 0 → n=M (divisible only by 3) ⇒ min s=9 ⇒ ratio 2/3 → g=2/3.  
c=4M → n=5M (3&5) ⇒ min s=9 ⇒ ratio 2/3 → g=10/3.  
c=1848374, 10162574: c+1=5³·31·53·… ⇒ n divisible by 25 (no 7,11) ⇒ ratio 16/25 → g=16/25 (twice).  
c=265710644: c+1=5·97·103·197·… ⇒ smallest s=97 ⇒ ratio 64/97 → g=64/97.  
c=44636594: c+1=5·103·167·173·… ⇒ s=103 ⇒ ratio 68/103 → g=68/103.  

Sum = 2/3+10/3+2·16/25+64/97+68/103 = 1648512/249775.  
p+q=1898287 → (p+q) mod 99991 = **98449**.  

Pitfalls: ensure s≥6, use scaling property f(d·s)=d·f(s); verify 2025! divisible by each denominator.

Insights: f(n)=min lcm(a,b,c) for a+b+c=n ⇒ optimal triples are chains (c multiple of a,b). Ratio r=c/(a+b+c) depends only on primitive sum s (smallest sum in its divisor class). Primitive sums ordered by increasing r: 11(6/11), 7(4/7), 17(10/17), 10(3/5), 23(14/23), 13(8/13), 29(18/29), 16(5/8), 19(12/19), … 9(2/3) later. For n=M+ c, M=3^{2025!}. If s coprime to 3, M≡1 (mod s) ⇒ s|n ⇔ s|(c+1). If s multiple of 3, s|n ⇔ s|M (i.e. s a power of 3). Small c’s give first divisor s: c=0→9 (r=2/3); 1848374→25 (16/25); 10162574→47 (30/47); 265710644→97 (64/97); 44636594→167 (110/167). For c=4M, n=5M, smallest s dividing is 9 ⇒ r=2/3, and g(4M)=5r=10/3 (floor adds 4r). For other c, floor term zero ⇒ g(c)=r. Sum = 2/3+10/3+16/25+30/47+64/97+110/167 = 125561848/19033825. p+q mod 99991 = 8687. Pitfalls: ensure s primitive (not multiple of earlier), handle 3‑divisible s, verify 2025! divisible by denominators.

Insights: f(n)=n·min_{d|n} (f(d)/d); global min ratio =6/11 (sum 11). For n=M (3^K) only 3‑powers divide → ratio 2/3. For n=M+4M=5M divisors are 3‑powers & 5·3^k → ratio 2/3. For n=M+c (c even, ≠0 mod 3) divisors are exactly the factors of c+1 not multiples of 3. Compute r(d)=f(d)/d for each divisor d (use pre‑computed f up to 3·10⁸ via brute‑force for small d). Minimal ratio = smallest r among those divisors. Then g(c)=⌊2025!·ratio⌋/2025!. Sum six g’s → rational p/q. Reduce, output (p+q) mod 99991. Pitfalls: ensure c+1’s 3‑free divisors only; handle M,4M separately (ratio 2/3). Use exact integer arithmetic.

Insights: f(n)=n·min_{S|n}R(S) where R(S)=min_{a+b+c=S}lcm(a,b,c)/S. Compute best R(S) for S≤2000 (R(11)=6/11, R(7)=4/7, R(9)=2/3, R(25)=16/25, R(47)=30/47, R(97)=64/97, R(167)=110/167).  

M=3^{2025!}≡1 (mod p≠3). For N=M+c (c≠0,4M) N is odd, not divisible by 3; its odd divisors = odd divisors of c+1 (excluding factor 3).  

c=0 → S=9 → g=2/3.  
c=4M → N=5M, S=9 → g=10/3.  
c=1848374 (c+1=3²·5³·31·53) → divisors include 25 → best S=25 → g=16/25.  
c=10162574 (c+1=3²·5²·31²·47) → divisors include 47 → best S=47 → g=30/47.  
c=265710644 (c+1=3³·5·97·103·197) → divisors include 97 → best S=97 → g=64/97.  
c=44636594 (c+1=3·5·103·167·173) → divisors include 167 → best S=167 → g=110/167.  

Sum = 2/3+10/3+16/25+30/47+64/97+110/167 = 125561848/19033825.  

p+q mod 99991 = 8687.  

Pitfalls: Assume N divisible by 3 (false for c≠0,4M); ignore larger S (e.g., 47,167) that give lower ratios.
